metadata.title: A Rational Protocol Treatment of 51% Attacks

editorial_review.merit_reason: Read the official CRYPTO conference text, focusing on Sections2–6, utility definitions and attack/mitigation theorem statements. It identifies a long-horizon payoff artifact, constructs bounded-horizon mining incentives and derives conditional double-spend profitability and confirmation-depth bounds. Assumptions include fixed-difficulty, bounded-delay mining, modeled costs/payoffs and eventual unprofitability. The mitigation provides attack-payoff security, explicitly not its strong variant, and trades longer confirmation delay for robustness. Ethereum Classic examples illustrate chosen parameters rather than independently validate all real attacks. This is substantive game-theoretic cryptographic security, not a pure consensus-engineering paper. Complete proofs are deferred to the full version; no proof audit or universal majority-attack protection is claimed.

metadata.title: Fair Distributed Computation of Reactive Functions

editorial_review.merit_reason: Read the author-hosted conference paper Sections 2–4, construction and bound statements; Edinburgh and Springer establish DISC 2015, ordered byline and pages 497–512. A designer–attacker game extends utility-based fairness to stateful reactive computation, with authenticated shared state and randomized output reconstruction. The construction is two-party, synchronous and sequentially composed; this is not an equilibrium among all rational participants. Optimality is parameter-dependent, with a non-tight regime. The conference text defers theorem proofs to the full ePrint, which returned 403; no proof audit is claimed. Corollary 1 and the preceding theorem print different threshold expressions, so no blanket optimality claim is endorsed. The substantive contribution fits game theory × cryptographic security independently of blockchain applications.

editorial_review.merit_reason: Read the institutional18-page manuscript, especially coercion/deception definitions, composition and constructions. It formalizes local counterstrategies against vote buyers/coercers and informants, without requiring coerced parties to coordinate or know the corrupt set. This user-nominated work is a strategic-security foundation for preventing enforceable vote buying, not a generic encryption application. It uses simulation-based coercion resistance rather than a utility-maximizing Nash analysis; no rational-participation equilibrium is claimed. Construction assumptions include honest tamper-resistant encryption tokens, broadcast, static coercion/corruption and t+t′<n; security permits abort, and inherent output leakage remains. Proofs are deferred to the full version, so this review does not certify them.

metadata.title: Profitable Manipulations of Cryptographic Self-Selection Are Statistically Detectable
metadata.venue: 6th Conference on Advances in Financial Technologies (AFT 2024)
metadata.abstract:
Cryptographic Self-Selection is a common primitive underlying leader-selection for Proof-of-Stake blockchain protocols. The concept was first popularized in Algorand [Jing Chen and Silvio Micali, 2019], who also observed that the protocol might be manipulable. [Matheus V. X. Ferreira et al., 2022] provide a concrete manipulation that is strictly profitable for a staker of any size (and also prove upper bounds on the gains from manipulation).

Separately, [Maryam Bahrani and S. Matthew Weinberg, 2024; Aviv Yaish et al., 2023] initiate the study of undetectable profitable manipulations of consensus protocols with a focus on the seminal Selfish Mining strategy [Eyal and Sirer, 2014] for Bitcoin’s Proof-of-Work longest-chain protocol. They design a Selfish Mining variant that, for sufficiently large miners, is strictly profitable yet also indistinguishable to an onlooker from routine latency (that is, a sufficiently large profit-maximizing miner could use their strategy to strictly profit over being honest in a way that still appears to the rest of the network as though everyone is honest but experiencing mildly higher latency. This avoids any risk of negatively impacting the value of the underlying cryptocurrency due to attack detection).

We investigate the detectability of profitable manipulations of the canonical cryptographic self-selection leader selection protocol introduced in [Jing Chen and Silvio Micali, 2019] and studied in [Matheus V. X. Ferreira et al., 2022], and establish that for any player with α < (3-√5)/2 ≈ 0.38 fraction of the total stake, every strictly profitable manipulation is statistically detectable. Specifically, we consider an onlooker who sees only the random seed of each round (and does not need to see any other broadcasts by any other players). We show that the distribution of the sequence of random seeds when any player is profitably manipulating the protocol is inconsistent with any distribution that could arise by honest stakers being offline or timing out (for a natural stylized model of honest timeouts).

editorial_review.merit_reason: Reviewed selected model, equilibrium, construction and impossibility sections of the author extended manuscript. It models a miner committing to off-chain auctions and users responding in Bayesian equilibrium, distinguishes on-chain simplicity from influence-proofness, and analyzes encrypted bids with miner-set reserves. Positive results rely on i.i.d. regular values, monopoly reserve and miner blindness to bid contents; they do not provide unconditional collusion resistance. Impossibility statements depend on the stipulated equilibrium/property combination. Cryptography is an abstract restriction on strategies, not a proved deployed MPC implementation. SIGecom and Crossref establish an EC2024 one-page abstract; the46-page author text supplies substantive review evidence and is not attributed wholesale to that page.
